tabs.note: Build order matters here: Tier 1 first (highest ROI, lowest KD, highest intent), Tier 3 in parallel with Tier 2, Tier 4 last. Every page in this plan needs: a 2-3 sentence quick-answer summary up top (what LLMs cite verbatim), FAQ schema, semantic-HTML comparison tables, and internal links that build a crawlable entity web across all 148 pages.
columns: Who Lands Here / What the Page Does / Why It Converts
rows: A buyer who has already shortlisted JAGGAER and one other vendor and is close to a decision. JAGGAER leads: honest head-to-head, acknowledge competitor strengths and JAGGAER's own limitations for trust, but structure the comparison so JAGGAER's differentiators land for the ICP (manufacturing, higher ed, public sector, enterprise complexity). Highest-intent query type in the set; KD 2-10 means fast ranking; directly drives demo requests.

A buyer comparing two competitors, JAGGAER not on their radar yet. Neutral, well-researched comparison; JAGGAER does not appear in headline or body. Close with: a line introducing JAGGAER as worth checking, linking to the relevant JAGGAER vs Competitor pages. Individually low-traffic, collectively significant — 105 chances to intercept a buyer mid-evaluation. GEO bonus: LLMs cite these pages when answering 'X vs Y' questions, surfacing JAGGAER even when it isn't the subject.

A buyer evaluating or already using a competitor, warm but uncommitted (e.g. 'Coupa alternatives' = unhappy, in renewal, or building a shortlist). A genuinely useful listicle of 6-8 alternatives; JAGGAER appears as a strong option with clear ICP positioning, not framed as the obvious winner. Feeds the funnel: Alternatives page to JAGGAER vs Competitor page to demo. Top volumes: tipalti alternatives (260/mo), ramp alternatives (210/mo), coupa alternatives (170/mo).

Long-term authority and GEO/AEO signal builder. 'Best procurement software for manufacturing' and 'for higher education' align with JAGGAER's strongest verticals. KD slightly higher (15-31) but still winnable. Longest shelf life; the pages LLMs cite when answering broad category questions.

• A 'quick answer' summary paragraph at the top of every page (2-3 sentences that directly answer the query) — this is what LLMs cite verbatim.
• Structured FAQ schema on every page — feeds Google AI Overviews and LLM responses directly.
• Comparison tables built with semantic HTML — structured data LLMs extract and reference.
• Internal links across all 148 pages that create a crawlable entity web around JAGGAER.

tabs.title: SEO Glossary — Plain-English Definitions
columns: What It Means (in the context of this workbook)
rows: A high-value search term directly tied to revenue — what JAGGAER actually wants to rank for and sell against (e.g. 'procurement software', 12,100 searches/month). These are also the hardest to rank for, since every competitor is chasing the same term. This plan deliberately does NOT write content targeting these 8 terms head-on.

The idea that Google trusts a website more on a subject the more comprehensively that site covers related terms. By publishing 50 pieces on adjacent, easier keywords, JAGGAER builds credibility across the whole procurement topic — which then helps the money keywords rank too, even though no content targets them directly.
How many times a keyword is searched on Google per month, on average. Higher volume = more potential traffic, but usually also more competition.

A 0-100 score estimating how hard it is to rank on page 1 of Google for a term, based on how strong the sites currently ranking are. Lower KD = easier to break into that SERP. This workbook only includes keywords under KD 28 because those are realistic, faster wins.

What the searcher actually wants when they type the term. 'Informational' = they want to learn something (e.g. 'what is procurement'). 'Commercial' = they're comparing or evaluating options and closer to a buying decision (e.g. 'best supplier management tools').

A grouping of the 50 keywords into 5 themed clusters (e.g. Supplier Management, Contract/CLM/RFx) purely for planning and production convenience — keywords in the same batch tend to link to each other naturally.
Search Engine Results Page — the page of results Google shows for a query. 'Ranking on page 1' means appearing in the SERP for that term.

A group of related articles that link to each other, usually anchored by one broad 'hub' piece and several narrower 'spoke' pieces. Google reads dense internal linking within a cluster as a signal of expertise on that topic.

A link from one page on JAGGAER's own site to another (e.g. a blog post linking to a product page). Internal links pass 'authority' from content pages to the commercial pages Netscribes wants to rank — this is the entire mechanism behind the 50-keyword strategy.
The specific next step the content asks the reader to take — usually 'request a demo' or 'see the platform' — paired with which JAGGAER page it should link to.
A secondary, related keyword woven naturally into a piece of content alongside its main topic, so one article can rank for several related searches at once instead of just one.

A simple way to compare keywords on 'traffic per unit of ranking effort.' A high score means strong search volume for relatively low difficulty — the best return on writing time. Used in the Quick Wins tab to prioritise.
Google's framework for judging content quality: Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness. Backlinks, credible sourcing, and genuine depth all feed into this.

A link from another website pointing to JAGGAER's content. Backlinks from credible sites (industry publications, analysts) are one of Google's strongest ranking signals — this is why formats like 'best practices guides' and listicles are favoured, as they attract more of them.
A long-form, comprehensive piece (2,500+ words) designed to rank for a broad term and act as the central internal-linking hub for a batch of narrower, related articles.

Optimising content to be surfaced and cited inside AI-generated answers (Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity) rather than just the traditional blue-link SERP. Added focus area from the Aug 11 2026 call, driven by a 20% drop in JAGGAER homepage clicks attributed to AI Overviews.

Google's AI-generated summary panel that now appears above traditional search results for many queries. If JAGGAER isn't cited inside the AIO panel for a term like 'procurement software,' traffic goes to whichever competitor or review site the AIO surfaces instead, even if JAGGAER ranks normally below it.

Funnel stages: Top of Funnel (awareness, informational), Middle of Funnel (consideration), Bottom of Funnel (BOFU — ready to evaluate or buy, commercial/navigational intent). Per the Aug 11 2026 call, BOFU content is now the priority because it is what drives GEO/AIO visibility.

Two separate tags, per the Aug 11 2026 call. Keyword Intent (Informational/Commercial) describes what the searcher wants when they type the term. Blog Intent (Top/Middle/Bottom) is an editorial decision about how the article itself is angled — a technically informational keyword can still be written as bottom-of-funnel content if the brief calls for it.

When two pages on the same site compete against each other for the same keyword instead of each ranking for something distinct, which can dilute both. Flagged on the Aug 11 2026 call regarding whether blog content should avoid the exact phrase 'procurement software' to protect the product page's ranking for that term.

A very specific, conversational search phrase (e.g. 'what is the best procurement analytics software for a manufacturing company in Germany') typical of how people phrase questions to AI tools. These don't show up in standard keyword-volume tools but are a growing share of GEO-driven traffic.
